contributions.statement: When the same skill or domain note is copied into more than one repo, pin the upstream version and fail the build when it moves: 1,841 of 2,462 linked copies (74.8%) landed near-verbatim, and 40.2% of the 1,295 copies that were never edited locally had already missed an upstream change.
contributions.evidence: §IV and §VI-A. Similarity ≥ 0.99 counts as near-verbatim. The 52.6% never-edited rate is right-censored (history to 4 May 2026, no time-since-adoption adjustment, §VIII). Link audit is 30 pairs in [0.1, 0.3) plus 30 below 0.1. Public repos with ≥10 stars and skills.sh skills with ≥20 installs only. No agent-outcome measure.
relative_to: 2608.10906 about half of public SKILL.md files are exact copies

contributions.statement: Schedule a pruning review for locally maintained skill files, because on first-to-last diffs additions outnumbered removals 6.1:1 during evolution and 2.7:1 overall (586 vs 221), while adoption-time edits were nearly balanced (1.1:1).
contributions.evidence: §VII-A, from the 444 coded endpoint diffs (188 linked, 256 unlinked) after a 340-line churn fence. Endpoint diffs hide add-then-remove churn (§III-D, §VIII). The add/remove labels have no reported kappa.
relative_to: documentation maintenance accretes rather than prunes (Aghajani et al. 2019, cited §VII-A)

contributions.statement: Do not treat rarely edited user-interaction, monitoring, and failure-handling sections as a checked behavioural contract: those labels appeared in 1.6%/1.2%, 0.5%/0.0%, and 5.9%/7.1% of coded diffs, and the coders published no agreement statistic for that field.
contributions.evidence: §VII-A and §III-D. Rates are on the stratified 444-diff sample, not the corpus. Low edit frequency does not show the rules are correct.
relative_to: 2608.08453 lint shared SKILL.md files before they move across hosts

reason: The missed-upstream rate on near-verbatim copies is a sync rule for skills shared across repos, and the 6.1:1 addition skew is a pruning rule on top of known documentation accretion. Neither result says a better-maintained skill makes an agent more correct.
